rows: Attached analytical inputs — not verified public Findex aggregates
Over 90% of Yemeni adults are financially excluded; severe gender gap where female ownership is approximately 3.8%.
Reflects severe banking sector retreat, institutional branch contraction, and physical branch concentration in primary urban hubs.
Fastest growing financial modality; driven by microfinance bank fintech initiatives (e.g. Kuraimi, Tadhamon, Al-Amal).
ATM infrastructure severely impaired by liquidity rationing, power grid collapse, and dual central bank banknotes.
Digital payments represent primary gateway to formal inclusion, but heavily skewed towards urban male transactions.
Telecom top-ups and private solar grid subscriptions drive over 70% of non-cash consumer digital transactions.
Merchant acceptance constrained by merchant reluctance to hold digital balances due to cash-out liquidity conversion fees.
Received Humanitarian / G2P Cash via Account
Aid-driven inclusion; WFP and social funds increasingly test e-vouchers and mobile wallets for food security transfers.
Can Access Emergency Funds in 30 Days
Severe vulnerability: >71% of Yemeni adults cannot mobilize 1/20th GNI per capita (~$30-50 USD) within a 30-day period.
Informal kinship networks represent the absolute primary social buffer, far exceeding accumulated liquid savings.
Acute household savings depletion resulting from hyper-inflation, currency collapse, and long-standing wage arrears.
Emergency Funds from Sale of Assets
Distress selling of productive assets (livestock, solar panels, family jewelry) is a widespread secondary coping mechanism.
High borrowing rate demonstrates high structural dependence on debt for daily consumption and food security.
Dominates the credit landscape; interest-free informal borrowing based on social capital and familial reciprocity.
Neighborhood grocery "credit notebooks" (Daftar) serve as the primary institutional buffer for household food security.
Extreme credit rationing; formal commercial and microfinance banks require physical gold or land collateral.
Poverty is the overriding constraint; individuals perceive formal banking as exclusive to businesses and wealthy elites.
Disproportionately excludes displaced women and youth lacking recognized national biometric ID or proof of address.
Barrier: Financial Services Too Far Away
High transport costs and physical road insecurity create prohibitive friction for rural populations seeking urban branches.
Barrier: Lack of Trust in Banks
Residual impact of bank liquidity freezes, historical deposit lockups, and conflicting dual central bank regulatory mandates.
